meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's not quite true that I had nothing on. I had the radio on'?
meta.ogDescription: Earliest known printing: Sheilah Graham's column, Evening Star, 23 June 1952 — "I had the radio on." The longer wording comes from Esquire, July 1953.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Monroe really did make this joke, and the paper trail is unusually good for a movie-star quip: it was in print by 23 June 1952, in Sheilah Graham’s syndicated Hollywood Diary, and she used it again for Bennett Cerf in Esquire in July 1953. What no source contains is this sentence pair. The 1952 columns print only the punchline, “I had the radio on”; the 1953 Esquire version runs “it’s not quite true I had nothing on: the radio was on.” The popular wording splices the two halves together.
answer.confidenceText: Attributed — the joke is documented from Monroe in 1952 and 1953, but this exact wording is a later splice of two of her own versions.

source.excerpt: A pompous visitor asked Marilyn Monroe at Niagara—“Is it true that when you posed for that famous calendar photograph, Miss Monroe, you had nothing on?” “No,” said our Marilyn, “I had the radio on.”
trail: Quote Investigator credits Monroe, with a caveat. Its survey of the quip ↗ traces versions through 1952 and 1953 and concludes that “Marilyn Monroe should receive credit for this quip,” naming Sheilah Graham’s June 1952 column as the earliest evidence known to QI. It also allows that a studio humorist may have crafted the line for her — while recording that she “definitely employed the quip” in the 1953 Esquire interview.

We pulled the 1952 newspaper page itself. The Library of Congress scan of the Evening Star for 23 June 1952 ↗ carries Sheilah Graham’s “Hollywood Diary” on page 13, and the item’s text ends on the punchline “I had the radio on.” That is the whole of the documented joke in its earliest form.

Wikiquote sources it — to the short form. The Marilyn Monroe article ↗ lists the quote as simply “I had the radio on,” citing “Something for the Boys,” Time 60, no. 6 (11 August 1952): 90. The longer sentence pair is not listed there either.

The popular wording is a splice. Comparing the printings side by side, its first half follows the July 1953 Esquire profile and its second half follows the 1952 newspaper columns. Every word is Monroe’s; the combination is not from any source we or Quote Investigator ↗ could locate.
source.excerptNote: Sheilah Graham, “Hollywood Diary,” Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), 23 June 1952, p. A-13, released by the North American Newspaper Alliance. Note what it does not contain: there is no “it’s not quite true that I had nothing on” clause anywhere in the item. That half of the famous wording only appears a year later, in Esquire, and in a different form.

source.rightsNote: Monroe’s remark survives only through what other people printed, and both key printings fall well after 1931: Sheilah Graham’s syndicated column of 23 June 1952 and Bennett Cerf’s Esquire profile of July 1953. The Library of Congress serves this Evening Star issue under a statement that it believes its newspapers are “in the public domain or have no known copyright restrictions,” but that same statement warns that issues published less than 95 years ago “may contain some copyrighted third party materials” — which is precisely what a syndicated wire column is. We therefore treat both printed texts as in copyright and quote only the short passages at issue.

author.name: Marilyn Monroe
author.heading: Who she was
author.bio: Born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles on 1 June 1926, Monroe went from photographic model to the most famous woman in American film, and was dead at 36 in August 1962. In 1949, years before the fame, she posed nude for photographer Tom Kelley — for a fee of $50 — and the images ran on John Baumgarth calendars under the name “Mona Monroe.” When the connection surfaced in 1952 her studio expected it to end her career; she declined to be embarrassed, and the line on this page is the form that refusal took.

misattribution.heading: The right person, the wrong sentence
misattribution.intro: Nobody seriously disputes that Marilyn Monroe made this joke — Quote Investigator credits her, and it was in print within months of the calendar scandal breaking. What travels online is a tidied-up wording that no 1952 or 1953 source actually prints, plus a set of confident assumptions about where and when she said it.

items.who: “It’s not quite true that I had nothing on. I had the radio on”
items.why: The first half tracks the July 1953 Esquire profile — “it’s not quite true I had nothing on: the radio was on” — while the second half is the newspaper punchline, “I had the radio on.” Both halves are Monroe’s, but QI, which reproduces both ↗, prints no version that joins them this way.

items.who: “She said it at a press conference”
items.why: The versions disagree about who did the asking. Graham has “a pompous visitor” on the Niagara location in June 1952; Louella Parsons, in February 1953, has a curious nurse asking while Monroe was ill with flu; Erskine Johnson merely says she was “asked just the other day.” QI prints all three ↗ and concludes she probably used the line on multiple occasions, so a single definitive occasion may not exist.

items.who: A studio publicist or gag writer
items.why: Quote Investigator raises this itself: “It is conceivable that this tale was crafted by a humorist on behalf of Monroe and her studio; the zinger was then given to Graham for publication.” It immediately adds that Monroe “definitely employed the quip” when interviewed for the July 1953 Esquire profile — so even if the line was written for her, she used it in her own voice. Read the full finding ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is genuinely Monroe’s. The earliest evidence known to Quote Investigator ↗ is Sheilah Graham’s column of 23 June 1952, where the punchline reads simply “I had the radio on” — and the fuller “it’s not quite true I had nothing on” phrasing comes from Bennett Cerf’s Esquire profile of July 1953. Quote either one. The spliced version belongs to nobody.

context.heading: Why the joke mattered
lead: In 1949, before anyone knew her name, Monroe posed nude for photographer Tom Kelley and the images ran on John Baumgarth calendars under the pseudonym “Mona Monroe.” When the connection surfaced in 1952, with Niagara in production, the studio’s instinct was containment: Louella Parsons reported in January 1952 that one of Monroe’s bosses was so alarmed that “an order was given to buy them up.”

Monroe refused the containment strategy. Her argument, Parsons wrote, was “art for art’s sake”; her answer in public was the radio line, which was circulating in the gossip columns by that June. Bennett Cerf’s Esquire profile recorded the outcome plainly: “The unpredictable public sided wholeheartedly with Marilyn in the ensuing hullabaloo.” Niagara was released in January 1953.
detailsBody: 23 June 1952 — Sheilah Graham, “Hollywood Diary,” Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), p. A-13. A “pompous visitor” asks her on the Niagara location; she answers “No … I had the radio on.” This is the earliest evidence known to Quote Investigator.
24 June 1952 — the same exchange runs as a filler item, “Day Brightener,” in the Minneapolis Morning Tribune, p. 27.
2 August 1952 — Erskine Johnson, The Daily Chronicle (De Kalb, Illinois), p. 6: “Sure, I had the radio on.” The same column puts her calendar fee at $50.
11 August 1952 — Time, “Something for the Boys,” p. 90, which Wikiquote cites for the short form “I had the radio on.”

2 February 1953 — Louella Parsons, The Philadelphia Inquirer, p. 15. A nurse asks her during a bout of flu; Monroe, “now thoroughly bored with this subject,” answers “Of course, it isn’t true … I had the radio on.”

July 1953 — Bennett Cerf, “The ‘Altogether’ Girl,” Esquire 40, no. 1, p. 93: “Sure, I posed that way. I needed the money. And it’s not quite true I had nothing on: the radio was on. Besides the artist’s wife was in the room all the time.”
None of the six is the sentence pair that circulates today.

Marilyn Monroe was born Norma Jeane Mortenson on 1 June 1926 in Los Angeles and died 4 August 1962 aged 36; she posed for nude photographs by Tom Kelley in 1949 for John Baumgarth calendars using the name "Mona Monroe"; the calendar became a public scandal in 1952; Niagara was released in January 1953.
Tom Kelley was the photographer of Marilyn Monroe's 1949 nude photographs and paid her $50 for the shoot.
